title: It's Not About the Axolotl
author: Jo Castellino
summary: Jo Castellino uses a vivid classroom scenario — a student thrown by an unfamiliar animal (an axolotl) appearing in an exam question about gas exchange — to diagnose a widespread error in how teachers respond to exam results: fixing the surface feature (adding axolotls to next year's curriculum) rather than the underlying problem (students cannot apply familiar knowledge to unfamiliar contexts). The axolotl question was not about axolotls; it was a gas exchange question presented through an unfamiliar example. The problem was not content coverage but transfer: students had learned about gas exchange only through the contexts used in class and could not recognize the concept when dressed in new clothing. Castellino argues this diagnostic error is systemic — teachers instinctively patch the knowledge gap they can see (the specific example) rather than addressing the teaching gap they cannot see (insufficient practice with novel application). The article is a precise account of the gap between learning content and learning to deploy content flexibly, with significant implications for how teachers design and sequence practice.
points: The 'axolotl problem' is a template for a universal teaching error: identifying a specific knowledge gap from an exam question and patching it with that specific content, when the real problem is students' inability to transfer knowledge to novel contexts.

Transfer — the capacity to recognize a familiar concept when it appears in an unfamiliar form — is the crucial skill exam questions test, but the least systematically taught; most classroom practice involves familiar contexts applied to familiar questions.

The diagnostic move that matters is asking 'why couldn't the student recognize this?' not 'what did the student not know?' — because the first question leads to pedagogy improvements, while the second leads to more content.

Teachers' instinct to add the specific example to next year's scheme is reasonable and understandable, but produces students who can answer exam questions about axolotls without being able to answer gas exchange questions using any new example.

The implication for curriculum and assessment design is significant: if students can only apply concepts in the contexts used in class, the curriculum should explicitly include varied-context practice — presenting known concepts in multiple unfamiliar applications — before the exam.
quotes: Martha is sat in the exam hall, waiting to be told she can start her Biology paper. She has revised for hours and attended every revision session.
They march straight to their teacher to tell her how they feel. She is taken aback by the strength of the reaction from Martha and her peers.
Luckily, the Year 11s have nearly finished, so she has more time to look over the curriculum. They won’t be able to say they haven’t been taught this next year.

How many times have we come across a question that asks students to apply a familiar idea in an unfamiliar context, only to spend the following year practising that exact style of question? We were making sure students were as well prepared as possible and giving them every chance to succeed by practising unusual application questions.

I don’t mean to get too philosophical, but are we teaching so students excel in their exams? Are we trying to make sure they memorise every possible fact, only for most of it to disappear a year later?

The irony is that I remember the percentage far more vividly than I remember the content of the exams or the lessons that came before them. If we see the curriculum as a sequence of facts to be taught, supported by hundreds of examples lifted from previous exam papers, then I think we risk undermining learning and everything education should be about.

We should ask students to apply them in a range of different scenarios and deliberately connect related ideas so they see both the bigger picture and the finer details [ ].
